content.text: Chapter 6 studies extended bodies as systems of particles, moving as a whole and through internal or rotational motion. An ideal rigid body has a definite, unchanging shape: distances between every pair of its particles remain constant. Real bodies deform, but many objects can be treated as rigid when deformation is negligible.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: In pure translation, all particles of a rigid body have the same velocity at any instant. In rotation about a fixed axis, every particle moves in a circle in a plane perpendicular to the axis, with the circle’s centre on the axis; points on the axis remain stationary. Rolling motion combines translation and rotation. A freely moving rigid body can translate or combine translation and rotation. A body fixed at one point or line is constrained to rotational motion; this chapter focuses on rotation about a fixed axis.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Translation and rotation of rigid bodies

content.text: For two particles of masses m1 and m2 at positions x1 and x2 on a line, the centre of mass is the mass-weighted mean of their positions. For equal masses, it lies midway between them.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Centre of mass of two particles

content.text: For n particles along the x-axis, the centre-of-mass coordinate is the sum of each mass multiplied by its coordinate, divided by total mass M. For particles in a plane or in space, calculate each coordinate in the same mass-weighted way.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Centre of mass of many particles

content.text: Using position vectors ri for each particle and R for the centre of mass, the centre-of-mass position is the mass-weighted vector average. If the origin is chosen at the centre of mass, the mass-weighted vector sum of positions is zero.
equations: Σ(mi ri) = 0 when the origin is at the centre of mass

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Vector form of centre of mass

content.text: An extended body can be approximated as a collection of small mass elements Δmi. In the continuous limit, sums become integrals and the centre of mass is found from integrals of position weighted by mass element. For homogeneous bodies with reflection symmetry, the centre of mass coincides with the geometric centre.
equations: X = (1/M)∫x dm; Y = (1/M)∫y dm; Z = (1/M)∫z dm

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Centre of mass of continuous bodies

content.text: The chapter illustrates centre-of-mass calculations for three particles at the vertices of an equilateral triangle with masses 100 g, 150 g and 200 g; a uniform triangular lamina, whose centre of mass lies at the concurrence of its medians; and a uniform L-shaped lamina formed from three equal unit squares. For the L-shaped example, the centre of mass is at (5/6 m, 5/6 m).
equations: For discrete masses: X = Σ(mi xi)/M; Y = Σ(mi yi)/M

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: For a system of constant total mass, differentiating the centre-of-mass position gives the relation between total momentum and centre-of-mass velocity. Differentiating again relates centre-of-mass acceleration to the vector sum of particle accelerations weighted by mass. Internal forces occur in equal and opposite pairs under Newton’s third law and cancel in the total force; only external forces determine centre-of-mass motion.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The centre of mass of a system moves as if all the system’s mass were concentrated there and all external forces acted at that point. Internal forces need not be known to determine the centre-of-mass motion. A projectile that explodes continues to have its centre of mass follow the trajectory set by external forces, such as gravity.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The linear momentum of a system is the vector sum of the momenta of its particles. It equals total mass multiplied by centre-of-mass velocity. The time rate of change of total momentum equals the total external force. If the total external force is zero, total linear momentum is conserved and the centre of mass moves with constant velocity.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The chapter uses radioactive decay and binary-star motion to illustrate momentum conservation and the centre-of-mass frame. When external forces are negligible, decay products move so that total momentum is unchanged; in the centre-of-mass frame, the centre of mass is at rest. Separating centre-of-mass motion from motion relative to the centre of mass simplifies system dynamics.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The vector product a × b has magnitude ab sin θ, is perpendicular to the plane containing a and b, and has direction determined by the right-handed screw or right-hand rule. It is non-commutative: a × b = −b × a. It is distributive over vector addition. A vector crossed with itself is zero; unit-vector products follow cyclic order: i × j = k, j × k = i, k × i = j, with reversed order giving negative results.
equations: a × (b + c) = a × b + a × c
a × b = (ay bz − az by)i + (az bx − ax bz)j + (ax by − ay bx)k

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The chapter gives vectors a = 3i − 4j + 5k and b = −2i + j − 3k. Their scalar product is −25 and their vector product is 7i − j − 5k; reversing the order changes the sign of the vector product.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: For a particle moving around a circle, average angular velocity is angular displacement divided by elapsed time; instantaneous angular velocity is dθ/dt. In rigid-body rotation about a fixed axis, all particles share the same angular velocity. Its vector direction is along the axis of rotation, set by the right-hand rule.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: For rotation about a fixed axis, a particle at perpendicular distance r⊥ from the axis has linear speed v = ωr⊥. In vector form, v = ω × r, where r is the position vector from an origin on the axis. The velocity is tangent to the particle’s circular path and perpendicular to both angular velocity and the perpendicular radius vector.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: Angular acceleration is the time rate of change of angular velocity. For rotation about a fixed axis, the direction of angular velocity is fixed and the vector relation reduces to the scalar relation α = dω/dt.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: Torque is the rotational analogue of force. For a force F applied at position vector r relative to an origin, torque is τ = r × F. Its magnitude is rF sin θ, or perpendicular distance from the origin to the line of action multiplied by force. Torque vanishes if force is zero, position vector is zero, or the force’s line of action passes through the origin. SI unit: N m; dimensions M L² T⁻². Torque is a vector, unlike work or energy.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: Angular momentum of a particle about an origin is the vector product of position and linear momentum. Its magnitude is r p sin θ, or perpendicular distance from the origin to the line of momentum multiplied by momentum. It vanishes when momentum is zero, the particle is at the origin, or the line of momentum passes through the origin.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: Differentiating l = r × p with respect to time gives the torque relation for a particle, since velocity crossed with momentum is zero. For a system, total angular momentum is the sum of individual angular momenta; under Newton’s third law with internal forces along the line joining particle pairs, internal torques cancel and the rate of change of total angular momentum equals total external torque.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Torque and change in angular momentum

content.text: If the total external torque on a system is zero, its total angular momentum remains constant. Vanishing total external force and vanishing total external torque are independent conditions; a couple has zero net force but nonzero torque.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: A rigid body is in mechanical equilibrium when both the net external force and the net external torque are zero. For coplanar forces, translational equilibrium requires zero sums of force components along two perpendicular axes, and rotational equilibrium requires zero net torque about an axis perpendicular to the plane.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces whose lines of action differ. Its net force is zero but it produces a torque. The moment of a couple is independent of the point about which moments are taken. A compass needle in Earth’s magnetic field is an example discussed in the chapter.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Couple and moment of a couple

content.text: The chapter discusses levers and asks the reader to identify fulcrum, effort, effort arm, load and load arm. In rotational equilibrium, clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance. The principle of moments also holds for parallel forces acting at an angle to the lever.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The centre of gravity is the point at which the total gravitational torque on a body is zero. In a uniform gravitational field, the centre of gravity coincides with the centre of mass. If gravitational acceleration varies across an extended body, the two points need not coincide. Centre of mass depends on mass distribution, not gravity.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The chapter analyses a ladder against a frictionless wall. Forces include the ladder’s weight acting at its centre of gravity, a wall reaction perpendicular to the wall, and a floor reaction resolved into normal force and friction. Equilibrium equations for forces and torque can determine the reactions and conditions preventing the ladder from slipping.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The moment of inertia of a body about an axis is the sum of each particle’s mass multiplied by the square of its perpendicular distance from the axis. It depends on how mass is distributed relative to the chosen axis. For a continuous body, the corresponding expression is an integral.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis with angular speed ω, each particle has speed vi = ωri. Summing the kinetic energies of all particles gives rotational kinetic energy in terms of moment of inertia.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: For a thin ring of mass M and radius R rotating about an axis through its centre perpendicular to its plane, all mass elements are distance R from the axis, so I = MR². The chapter also considers a light rod with two masses rotating about an axis through the system’s centre of mass and compares different mass distributions.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: Rotational kinematics parallels translational kinematics for motion with constant angular acceleration. Angular displacement θ, angular velocity ω and angular acceleration α play roles analogous to displacement, velocity and acceleration. Angular displacement is measured from a fixed reference direction; angle in radians is dimensionless.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Kinematics of rotational motion about a fixed axis

content.text: For rotation about a fixed axis with constant angular acceleration, the rotational equations mirror the standard constant-acceleration equations for linear motion.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: Convert revolutions to radians using 1 revolution = 2π radians. Angular speed in rad/s is 2π times the number of revolutions per second, or 2π times revolutions per minute divided by 60. The chapter’s engine example calculates angular acceleration, angular displacement and number of revolutions from initial and final angular speeds.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: For rotation about a fixed axis, the component of force perpendicular to the axis can produce torque about the axis. The rotational analogue of Newton’s second law relates net torque about the axis to angular acceleration and moment of inertia.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, a torque does work through angular displacement. The rate of doing work is rotational power. With constant moment of inertia, the work done by the net torque changes rotational kinetic energy.
equations: W = ∫τ dθ (for torque along the axis)

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Work done by torque and power

content.text: For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis that is also an axis of symmetry, angular momentum along the axis is L = Iω. Angular momentum and angular velocity are not generally parallel vectors, but the chapter’s stated relation applies to the simpler symmetric fixed-axis situations. Only the torque component along the fixed axis changes the axial angular momentum.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: When external torque about the rotation axis is zero, Iω remains constant for the situations discussed. Moving mass closer to the axis decreases moment of inertia and increases angular speed; moving mass farther away increases moment of inertia and decreases angular speed. The chapter connects this principle with a rotating chair, acrobats, divers, skaters and dancers.

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion
metadata.topic: Rotational conservation and changing moment of inertia

content.text: The chapter summary covers rigid-body motion; centre of mass; momentum and its conservation; cross products; angular velocity and linear velocity; torque and angular momentum; mechanical equilibrium; centre of gravity; moment of inertia; rotational kinetic energy; and angular momentum in fixed-axis rotation. Key relations include R = Σ(mi ri)/M, P = MV, dP/dt = Fext, dL/dt = τext, ΣF = 0, Στ = 0, I = Σ(mi ri²), and K = (1/2)Iω².

metadata.subject: Physics
metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: The textbook highlights that centre-of-mass motion depends only on external forces; system kinetic energy can be separated into centre-of-mass kinetic energy and kinetic energy relative to the centre of mass; system laws rely on Newton’s second and third laws; net external force and torque conditions are independent; total torque is origin-independent when net external force is zero; and centre of gravity equals centre of mass only in a uniform gravitational field.

metadata.chapter: Systems of Particles and Rotational Motion

content.text: Give the location of the centre of mass of a (i) sphere, (ii) cylinder, (iii) ring, and (iv) cube, each of uniform mass density. Does the centre of mass of a body necessarily lie inside the body?

Find the approximate location of the CM of the molecule, given that a chlorine atom is about 35.5 times as massive as a hydrogen atom and nearly all the mass of an atom is concentrated in its nucleus.

The angles made by the strings with the vertical are 36.9° and 53.1° respectively. The bar is 2 m long. Calculate the distance d of the centre of gravity of the bar from its left end.

The cylinder is free to rotate about its standard axis of symmetry, and the sphere is free to rotate about an axis passing through its centre. Which of the two will acquire a greater angular speed after a given time?
